documents: Huang et al. 2022, Geophys. J. Int. 229, 1212-1231 (published PDF, pp. 1212-1231, including supporting-information captions)

entry.evidence: their sensitivities to azimuthal anisotropy at MTZ depths remain unexplored

steps.action: Review MTZ anisotropy evidence from shear wave splitting, surface waves, normal modes, converted phases and focal mechanisms, with model amplitudes of about 1-2 per cent.
steps.quote: At MTZ depths, evidence for seismic anisotropy is more limited, but consistently reported from multiple methods

steps.action: Recall the authors' earlier SS-precursor estimate of about 3 per cent MTZ anisotropy beneath stacked subduction zones and under 1 per cent globally.
steps.quote: Our previous study using SS precursors (Huang et al. 2019) also presented regional evidence for 3 per cent azimuthal anisotropy

steps.action: Pose the question of how sensitive SS precursors are to azimuthal anisotropy at MTZ depths, motivated by geodynamic and mineral physics predictions.
steps.quote: their sensitivities to azimuthal anisotropy at MTZ depths remain unexplored

steps.action: Expand the hand-picked global SS data set (events 1988-2017, depth 0-75 km), apply an SNR cut of 2.5, filter at 15-50 s and use transverse components.
steps.quote: The final SS data set consists of 58 566 seismograms.

steps.action: Build 3-D SPECFEM3D_GLOBE synthetics: 13 sources, a dense array, realistic Peterson noise, and the same processing as the data.
steps.quote: to compute 3-D synthetic SS precursor waveforms

steps.action: Design synthetic experiments for two densely sampled regions, central Pacific (plume) and Japan (slab), with idealized and realistic geometries, three depth layers and 1/3/5 per cent anisotropy.
steps.quote: The goal was to simulate the azimuthal anisotropy generated by a mantle plume versus a subducting slab.

steps.action: Apply the Schmerr & Garnero (2006) stacking with moveout corrections, distance exclusion windows and bootstrap errors, plus the traveltime and amplitude corrections of Huang et al. (2019).
steps.quote: Full details regarding traveltime and amplitude correction methods are contained in Huang et al. (2019).

steps.action: Set up a grid-search inversion of SdS azimuthal traveltimes and amplitudes for Gc and Gs, giving strength and fast direction with chi-squared uncertainties.
steps.quote: we used a grid-search method to find the best-fitting Gc and Gs values

steps.action: Compute with noise-free synthetics what anisotropy in the shallow upper mantle, the deep upper mantle and the MTZ predicts for the five differential measurements (tests 1-3).
steps.quote: SS precursors can distinguish the depths of anisotropy structures based on the combinations of five differential traveltime and amplitude ratio measurements

steps.action: Test two-layer models (upper mantle plus MTZ, and two MTZ sublayers, Figs S1-S2) to check that S660S-S410S time is free of upper-mantle contamination; sublayers cannot be resolved.
steps.quote: we can use these measurements to detect MTZ anisotropy unambiguously without contaminations from upper mantle anisotropy

steps.action: Characterize detection thresholds by varying the strength and lateral size (10, 5, 2.5 degrees) of MTZ anisotropy against noise-based uncertainties at SNR = 7.
steps.quote: the S660S−SS and S660S−S410S times can both detect ≥3 per cent anisotropy

steps.action: Stack central Pacific data and synthetics in 30-degree azimuthal bins around the Hawaiian hotspot.
steps.quote: both S410S and S660S are clearly observed in data (Fig. 8c) and synthetics (Fig. 8d) from azimuthal stacking

steps.action: Invert central Pacific S660S-S410S times and SdS amplitudes; no estimate is significantly above zero.
steps.quote: this signal (dlnG = 2.9 ± 3.4 per cent) is not significantly above zero due to the large uncertainty

steps.action: Run a resolution test with noisy synthetics (SNR values) and idealized and realistic geometries, using a misfit parameter epsilon, to set the minimum detectable anisotropy (Fig. 10, Fig. S3).
steps.quote: To further test the weak anisotropy hypothesis, we added noise to the 3-D synthetics

steps.action: Conclude that central Pacific MTZ anisotropy is below the resolvable 3 per cent.
steps.quote: the azimuthal anisotropy in this region is likely to be smaller than 3 per cent

steps.action: Ask where the stacked circum-Pacific subduction signal of Huang et al. (2019) originates, and choose the Honshu/NE China flat-slab region.
steps.quote: there was ambiguity about where the signal originated, or if it was ubiquitous amongst all subduction zones

steps.action: Stack Japan subduction zone data and synthetics in four usable 30-degree azimuthal bins despite poor east-west coverage.
steps.quote: the S410S and S660S are still recovered from stacking in all these four bins

steps.action: Invert Japan S660S-S410S times with EARA2014 corrections, giving significant anisotropy with a trench-perpendicular fast direction of 93 ± 5 degrees.
steps.quote: strong MTZ anisotropy (dlnG = 15.3 ± 2.7 per cent) exists in this region with a trench-perpendicular fast direction

steps.action: Repeat the inversion with FWEA18 and S40RTS tomography corrections; strength varies (11.4 to 17.5 per cent), direction is stable, and all results are significant (Figs S4-S6).
steps.quote: To test if our result is biased by the EARA2014 model, we also used another high-resolution tomography model FWEA18

steps.action: Enlarge the uncertainty to include the spread between tomography corrections: 15.3 ± 9.2 per cent.
steps.quote: we recomputed the uncertainty of dlnG by accounting for the VS uncertainties from the tomography models

steps.action: Invert Japan S410S/SS and S660S/SS amplitudes; S410S/SS is significant and consistent with the traveltime result, suggesting upper-MTZ anisotropy.
steps.quote: The strength of anisotropy (dlnG = 19.2 ± 18.0 per cent) inverted from S410S/SS amplitudes is significantly above zero

steps.action: Test the amplitude result with the two alternative tomography models; it is no longer significant (Fig. S7).
steps.quote: the inversions for S410S/SS amplitudes based on other two tomography models are not significantly above zero

steps.action: Withdraw the amplitude-based localization of anisotropy below 410 km from interpretation.
steps.quote: the MTZ anisotropy constrained from S410S/SS amplitudes is not a robust signal, and this should not be used for further interpretations

steps.action: Run a resolution test for Japan with idealized and realistic geometries and stronger input anisotropy (Fig. 13).
steps.quote: S660S−S410S time can detect ∼15 per cent anisotropy with intermediate level of noise (SNR = 7)

steps.action: Retain the Japan MTZ anisotropy from traveltimes as robust.
steps.quote: This resolution test and chi-squared statistical test both suggest that the MTZ anisotropy observed in the Japan subduction zone is a robust feature.

steps.action: State the method's characterized resolution (traveltimes at least 3 per cent, amplitudes at least 5 per cent, about 1000 km lateral) and its coverage requirement of 4-5 azimuths with NR > 100.
steps.quote: The traveltimes of SS precursors can detect ≥3 per cent azimuthal anisotropy in the MTZ with intermediate level of noise (SNR = 7).

steps.action: Compare the central Pacific non-detection with three higher-mode surface wave models at 500 km depth, which show 0.5-1.0 per cent.
steps.quote: These three models only show 0.5–1.0 per cent azimuthal anisotropy near Hawaiian hot spot.

steps.action: Interpret the result to mean that Hawaiian plume flow has produced no significant MTZ azimuthal anisotropy.
steps.quote: the vertical mantle flow associated with the Hawaiian plume has not produced significant MTZ azimuthal anisotropy

steps.action: List rival mechanisms for the strong Japan signal: LPO of wadsleyite, metastable olivine, magnesite, stishovite, akimotoite, hydrous phases or ice-VII, and SPO of basaltic layering.
steps.quote: it is likely that more than one mineralogical mechanism contributed to these complex systems

steps.action: Exclude single-mineral LPO as a sole explanation, using cited abundance and elasticity estimates that give under 1 per cent or under 6 per cent.
steps.quote: the LPO of highly anisotropic minerals within the slab alone do not seem to explain the strong MTZ anisotropy either

steps.action: Keep grain-scale SPO of basaltic material, compatible with the roughly 6 per cent lower bound, as the plausible mechanism, possibly combined with LPO.
steps.quote: slab is a plausible mechanism to explain the strong MTZ anisotropy beneath NE China

steps.action: Compare the fast direction with source-side shear wave splitting and P-wave anisotropic tomography beneath NE China, and contrast it with other subduction zones.
steps.quote: The trench-perpendicular fast direction is consistent with previous observations using source-side shear wave splitting measurements

steps.action: Infer trench-parallel subslab MTZ flow from the inherited 3 per cent subslab anisotropy under a [001](010) wadsleyite slip system; the result agrees with geodynamic modelling (Faccenda 2014).
steps.quote: the seismic trench-perpendicular fast direction then infers trench-parallel flow in the subslab MTZ

steps.action: Conclude: significant Japan MTZ anisotropy with a trench-perpendicular fast direction attributed mainly to SPO, and central Pacific MTZ anisotropy below the detection threshold.
steps.quote: we detected significant azimuthal anisotropy (dlnG = 15.3 ± 9.2 per cent) with a trench-perpendicular fast direction

tree.answer: MTZ azimuthal anisotropy, reported by several methods but poorly constrained
No; inferred from stacked SdS traveltimes and amplitudes through a forward model
Characterize SS-precursor sensitivity, then estimate MTZ anisotropy in two regions
Depth of origin (shallow upper mantle, deep upper mantle, MTZ); for Japan, LPO of various minerals versus SPO
Yes for depth: synthetics show distinct measurement patterns per layer; mechanism rivals are separated only by magnitude arguments
Found: two densely sampled natural regions (plume versus flat slab)
Japan traveltime result survives alternative tomography corrections and resolution tests; amplitude result does not
Japan 15.3 ± 9.2 per cent kept; central Pacific under 3 per cent; SPO a plausible mechanism
No review file supplied; acknowledgements thank the editor and reviewers

end.claim: SS-precursor S660S-S410S times resolve significant MTZ azimuthal anisotropy of 15.3 ± 9.2 per cent with a trench-perpendicular fast direction (93 ± 5 degrees) beneath the NE China flat slab, and show no detectable (under 3 per cent) MTZ anisotropy beneath the central Pacific.

decisive_move.sentence: The 3-D synthetic depth tests showed that the S660S-S410S time is an independent measure of MTZ anisotropy, free of upper-mantle contamination; without this neither regional estimate could be attributed to the MTZ.

gates.evidence: The plume-versus-slab framing selected the study regions (p. 1214), but the data were an existing hand-picked catalogue, not acquired for a hypothesis. The Japan estimate faced chi-squared tests against zero anisotropy and resolution tests that could fail; the central Pacific inversion did fail to detect anisotropy, and the S410S/SS amplitude signal failed the tomography robustness test (pp. 1219, 1222-1223). Nothing is stated as fixed before the data; the epsilon < 1 detectability criterion is defined in the Results (p. 1220).

imports.item: Chi-squared misfit with p-value uncertainty estimation in the grid search
HPC cluster runs of about 4 hours on 384 CPUs per simulation

novelty_claims.quote: their sensitivities to azimuthal anisotropy at MTZ depths remain unexplored
[...] shear wave splitting measurements, SS precursors can distinguish the depths of anisotropy structures
SS precursors can serve as a new method to constrain seismic anisotropy in the upper and mid-mantle

limits: The headline claim (Japan estimate) is estimate_with_resolution. Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) the method's resolution (at least 3 per cent from traveltimes at SNR = 7 with NR > 100 per bin; at least 5 per cent from amplitudes) is capability_characterized; (b) the central Pacific result is an upper bound (under 3 per cent), estimate_with_resolution; (c) grain-scale SPO of basalt as the mechanism is best_explanation, reached by magnitude and abundance arguments from cited mineral physics, not by a crucial test; (d) trench-parallel subslab flow is conditional on an assumed wadsleyite slip system and reuses inherited Huang et al. (2019) data, and the alternative slip system is only argued against. Process limits: the supplement (Figs S1-S7) was not supplied, so the steps placed after the tests they support are coded from captions and main-text references. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgements say editor and reviewer suggestions 'helped improve the manuscript significantly', and the received/revised dates (May to Nov 2021) imply revision, but what changed is unknown (inference). The Japan estimate rests on four azimuthal bins, one with NR = 3, so the fit has few degrees of freedom. Uniform whole-MTZ anisotropy is assumed because sublayers cannot be resolved. Composition: capability_first fits only loosely; the method is characterized first and the phenomenon is then measured, but rivals about depth exist from the start.

disagreements.target: Huang et al. (2019), the authors' own stacked circum-Pacific subduction result
disagreements.support: Regional stacking of Japan alone shows the earlier trench-perpendicular pattern may be biased by the densely sampled Japan and South America regions, and that fast directions are heterogeneous across subduction zones.
disagreements.quote: our data could have been biased by the regions in Japan and South America where the data coverage is the densest

disagreements.target: Attribution of subduction-zone MTZ anisotropy to LPO of wadsleyite (Kawazoe et al. 2013)
disagreements.support: The roughly 6 per cent lower bound of the observed anisotropy exceeds what LPO of wadsleyite alone can explain, especially with added water.
disagreements.quote: a > 6 per cent anisotropy signal cannot be readily explained solely by LPO of wadsleyite

disagreements.target: Shear wave splitting and higher-mode surface waves as the main tools for deep mantle anisotropy
disagreements.support: Splitting lacks vertical resolution and surface waves have about 6500 km horizontal resolution, whereas SS precursors resolve depth with about 1000 km Fresnel zones.
disagreements.quote: the shear wave splitting method has limited vertical resolution to distinguish the depth distribution of anisotropy

disagreements.target: Akimotoite as a contributor to MTZ anisotropy (Shiraishi et al. 2008; Hao et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: A cited volume fraction of about 15 per cent in harzburgite would yield less than 1 per cent anisotropy, too little for the NE China signal.
disagreements.quote: thereby again yielding less than 1 per cent anisotropy in the MTZ

alternatives_considered.reason: Global models smooth structure and underestimate slab VS anomalies

alternatives_considered.chosen: S660S-S410S time for the anisotropy inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: They can be contaminated by upper mantle anisotropy

alternatives_considered.chosen: Traveltime-based estimate; S410S/SS amplitude result not interpreted
alternatives_considered.reason: Amplitude results have larger uncertainties and are not robust to the tomography model

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both idealized and realistic source-receiver geometries
alternatives_considered.reason: To mimic the actual azimuthal coverage of the data

alternatives_considered.chosen: Uniform anisotropy across the whole MTZ
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Anisotropy localized in the upper or lower MTZ sublayer

alternatives_considered.chosen: Grain-scale SPO of basaltic materials in the flat slab
alternatives_considered.alternatives: LPO of wadsleyite, metastable olivine wedge, magnesite, stishovite, akimotoite, hydrous phases or ice-VII
alternatives_considered.reason: Expected abundances and elasticity give too little anisotropy; SPO reaches about 6 per cent, matching the lower bound

alternatives_considered.chosen: [001](010) slip system of wadsleyite (Kawazoe et al. 2013)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A different slip system (e.g. Demouchy et al. 2011)
